### example-targets Phase 5 step 1: PreparedTarget names its work directory and its blocker, so the controls and the verifier stop relying on route.py's layout

Request 7 of the example-targets brief's Phase 5 step 1. interfaces.py appends two optional fields to PreparedTarget, workdir and blocker, both None by default, an additive change. runtime.prepare() now records the preparation's absolute directory in workdir, on every preparation made once that directory exists, failed ones included, and writes it to prepared.json. A failed preparation's blocker (stage, command, diagnostic, needs, next) moves out of source, which claims are bound to, into its own field, and runtime_slice.py reads it there. run_controls and run_verifier find a preparation by its workdir, still only if its prepared.json matches; one without a directory is a not-started record, never run.

Reproducer: three new tests failed first: the frozen field order in test_interfaces.py, a preparation that names its directory outside source, and controls run from a preparation outside &lt;attempt>/prepare/&lt;revision>, which runtime used to refuse. The existing tests that read source["blocker"] now read the field. The cache-hit test compares two preparations without their directories, which differ by design. example-targets-integration.sh exits 0: the contract (16), the targets suite (195), test_build.py (190), test_pipeline.py (29) and build.py --plan.

The brief is out of date on one point. Its request 7 says workdir would let ingestion stop deriving the preparation from route.py's layout, and bundle raw stdout and stderr. In fact ingestion never read a preparation's directory. The raw streams are relative to the attempt's directory, which workdir doesn't give, so ingestion still bundles none. That goes on the for-review list (Progress).

### example-targets Phase 5 step 1: one oracle convention, so the runner can drive the seven packets' controls and ingestion reads them right

change `kmqzoyplqrxk` · [log `7efb17b82cda`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/051e402b-750c-4a9d-bdd2-24dfb39add84/7efb17b82cda691603414f20c85c1b231b17535a4a409888829b7e56ca2461fd.jsonl.gz)

Request 9 of llm-dlc/loops/example-targets.md's Phase 5 step 1. The merged runner (runtime.run_controls) took a driver's inputs from the oracle's PROBES list and expected one echoed 'input' line per argument; ingestion read each revision with check(lines) as (input, problem) pairs. None of the seven packets (105, 285-287, 305-307) followed that: they define argv() and check() with other signatures, their drivers print an identity line or take two arguments per probe, the preparation copied oracle.py without the probes file it reads, and 285-287's check() returns a dict that ingestion read as character pairs, so a fixed release would have counted as violating. 105's PROBES was a Path, which would have raised a TypeError instead of a refusal.

The convention, in runtime.py's docstring: an oracle's driver_args() gives the driver's whole argument vector (else PROBES, the fixture's form, unchanged), every JSON line is kept and the oracle matches lines to probes itself; ingestion calls problems(lines) (else check), and a result that is not a list of (input, problem) pairs, or a SystemExit, is an error, never a verdict; the preparation locks and copies the sidecar's probe and trigger files beside the oracle, refusing a path out of the work directory. Each of the seven oracles gains driver_args() (equal to its argv command) and problems(lines) over its unchanged logic; 105's reads the Javadoc's contract without its declared deviations, so before violates at (-2)^31 and after holds, as its exact-fix pair expects. Each packet's example.json has a note; the index is regenerated.
